Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $p,q\in[1,\infty]$ be
conjugate exponents, and let $f,g$ be measurable real-valued functions.

1. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $q<\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^q(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_p\|g\|_q.$$
2. If $p=1$ and $q=\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$ and
   $g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_1\|g\|_\infty.$$
3. If $p=\infty$ and $q=1$ with $f\in L^\infty(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\|g\|_1.$$

In every case the right-hand side is finite, so $fg$ is integrable.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, let $k\in\mathbb N_0$, let $1\le p\le\infty$, and let
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$.

Every $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ belongs to
$W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$. Indeed $\varphi$ is bounded with compact support,
hence lies in $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ for every exponent in range, and each of
its classical partial derivatives is again smooth and compactly supported,
hence lies in $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and is the corresponding weak derivative
by [[lem-classical-derivatives-are-weak-derivatives]].

Define the **zero-boundary Sobolev space**
$$W_0^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K):=\overline{C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)},$$
the closure taken in the normed space
$(W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K),\|\cdot\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)})$ of
[[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]. The norm is a genuine norm on classes
by [[lem-sobolev-norm-is-well-defined-and-definite]], so this is the usual
metric closure of a subset of a normed space: $u\in W_0^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$
if and only if for every $\delta>0$ there is
$\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with
$\|u-\varphi\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}<\delta$. Write
$H_0^k(\Omega):=W_0^{k,2}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ when the scalar field is fixed by
context.

Three warnings are part of the definition. First, this is a closure of
almost-everywhere classes, and all its equalities are equalities of Sobolev
classes. Second, no pointwise boundary values and no trace characterization
are asserted: a description of $W_0^{k,p}$ by vanishing boundary data belongs
to the later trace theory and is not used here. Third, the closure is defined
for every $1\le p\le\infty$, but for $p=\infty$ it is not claimed that every
compactly supported $W^{k,\infty}(\Omega)$ function lies in $W_0^{k,\infty}(\Omega)$;
the definition merely names the closure of the test functions.

Let $m \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge 1$ and let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$.

1. **Fundamental theorem, second part, in $\mathbb{R}^{m}$.** Let
   $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ be differentiable at every point of $[a,b]$ as
   a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]), and
   suppose $f' : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ is integrable. Then
   $$\int_a^b f' \;=\; f(b) - f(a).$$
2. **A bounded derivative gives a Lipschitz function.** Let
   $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable at
   every point of $(a,b)$, and let $M \ge 0$ satisfy
   $\lVert f'(t)\rVert_2 \le M$ for every $t \in (a,b)$. Then
   $$\lVert f(t) - f(s)\rVert_2 \;\le\; M\,|t-s| \qquad \text{for all } s,t \in [a,b],$$
   that is, $f$ is Lipschitz with constant $M$ as a map
   $([a,b], d_{\mathbb{R}}) \to (\mathbb{R}^{m}, d_2)$
   ([[def-lipschitz-holder-contraction]], [[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]],
   [[lem-metrics-on-rn]]).

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Apply Holder with exponents $3,2,6$ from [F2] to each integral in [F3]. This gives $|c(a;b,w)|\le\frac12\|a\|_3(\|\nabla b\|_2\|w\|_6+\|\nabla w\|_2\|b\|_6)$, so step 1.1 proves the stated bound and continuity.

Let $D\subset\mathbb R^d$ be a nonempty bounded connected Lipschitz domain, $d\in\{2,3\}$, and let $\nu>0$. Use $V=H^1_0(D;\mathbb R^d)$ and $Q=L^2_0(D)$ from [[def-na-stokes-zero-mean-pressure-and-velocity-spaces]], the viscosity form $a_\nu(v,w)=2\nu\int_D\varepsilon(v):\varepsilon(w)$, and the form $c$ from [[def-na-evolutionary-skew-convective-form]]. Set
$$V_\sigma=\{v\in V:\operatorname{div}v=0\text{ in }L^2(D)\},\qquad H_\sigma=\overline{V_\sigma}^{\,L^2(D)}.$$
For $f\in L^2(0,T;L^2(D;\mathbb R^d))$ and $u_0\in H_\sigma$, an **energy weak solution** is a velocity $u\in L^\infty(0,T;H_\sigma)\cap L^2(0,T;V_\sigma)$, weakly continuous into $H_\sigma$, and a pressure $p\in L^{4/3}(0,T;Q)$ with zero spatial mean a.e., such that $\operatorname{div}u=0$ a.e. and, for every $\varphi\in C^1([0,T];V)$ vanishing near $T$,
$$-\int_0^T(u,\partial_t\varphi)_{L^2}\,dt+\int_0^T\big(a_\nu(u,\varphi)+c(u;u,\varphi)+b(\varphi,p)\big)\,dt=\int_0^T(f,\varphi)_{L^2}\,dt+(u_0,\varphi(0))_{L^2}.$$
It also satisfies, for almost every $t\in(0,T)$,
$$\frac12\|u(t)\|_{L^2}^2+\nu\int_0^t\|\nabla u(s)\|_{L^2}^2\,ds\le\frac12\|u_0\|_{L^2}^2+\int_0^t(f(s),u(s))_{L^2}\,ds.$$
No uniqueness is included in this definition. The formulation uses the real duality convention of [[def-pe12-gelfand-triple]].

Let $V$ be a separable reflexive real Banach space, let $H$ be a real Hilbert
space, and let $i:V\to H$ be an injective continuous linear map with dense
range. Let $V^*$ be the continuous real dual of $V$ and write
$\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{V^*,V}$ for its pairing with $V$. The canonical
map $J:H\to V^*$ is
$$J h(v)=(h,iv)_H\qquad(h\in H,\ v\in V).$$
It is continuous because $|Jh(v)|\le \|h\|_H\|i\|\|v\|_V$, and injective
because $i(V)$ is dense in $H$. A triple $(V,H,J)$ with these properties is
a **Banach evolution triple**. If $V$ is Hilbert, this is the real evolution
triple of [[def-parabolic-evolution-triple-and-energy-space]].

For $1<p<\infty$, $L^p(0,T;V)$ denotes the Bochner space of strongly
measurable $V$-valued functions with finite $p$th power norm, and
$p'=p/(p-1)$. For $u\in L^p(0,T;V)$ and $g\in L^{p'}(0,T;V^*)$, say
$g=u'$ in the distributional time sense if
$$\int_0^T (iu(t),iv)_H\,\phi'(t)\,dt =-\int_0^T\langle g(t),v\rangle_{V^*,V}\,\phi(t)\,dt$$
for every $v\in V$ and $\phi\in C_c^\infty(0,T)$. Define
$$W_p(0,T;V)=\{u\in L^p(0,T;V):u'\in L^{p'}(0,T;V^*)\}.$$
This definition assigns no endpoint values; a separate chain-rule theorem is
needed before evaluating a function in this space at an endpoint.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and $X$ a real or complex
Banach space. A strongly measurable function $f:\Omega\to X$ is
**Bochner integrable** if there is a sequence of integrable $X$-valued simple
functions $(s_n)$ such that

$$\lim_{n\to\infty}\int_\Omega\|f-s_n\|\,d\mu=0.$$

For such a sequence define

$$\int_\Omega f\,d\mu:=\lim_{n\to\infty}\int_\Omega s_n\,d\mu.$$

The displayed norm limit exists: the simple integral inequality gives

$$\left\|\int s_n-\int s_m\right\|\leq\int\|s_n-s_m\|\leq\int\|s_n-f\|+\int\|f-s_m\|,$$

so the simple integrals form a Cauchy sequence, and $X$ is complete. The next
theorem proves that the value is independent of the approximating sequence and
characterizes existence by integrability of $\|f\|$.

For $E\in\mathcal A$, write
$\int_Ef\,d\mu:=\int_\Omega\mathbf1_Ef\,d\mu$ whenever this function is
Bochner integrable.

Let $f:\Omega\to X$ be strongly measurable. Then $f$ is Bochner integrable if
and only if

$$\int_\Omega\|f\|\,d\mu<\infty.$$

Here an a.e.-defined scalar function is integrated through any measurable
representative supplied by the strong simple approximation. Moreover the
Bochner integral is independent of the approximating sequence in its
definition.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $p,q\in[1,\infty]$ be
conjugate exponents, and let $f,g$ be measurable real-valued functions.

   $g\in\mathcal L^q(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_p\|g\|_q.$$
2. If $p=1$ and $q=\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$ and
   $g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_1\|g\|_\infty.$$
3. If $p=\infty$ and $q=1$ with $f\in L^\infty(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\|g\|_1.$$

In every case the right-hand side is finite, so $fg$ is integrable.

$$S^1_h=\{w\in C^0(\overline D):w|_K\in P_1(K)\},\quad S^1_{h,0}=S^1_h\cap H^1_0(D).$$
The **mini-element spaces** are
$$V_h=[S^1_{h,0}]^d\oplus\bigoplus_{K\in\mathcal T_h}b_K\mathbb R^d\subset H^1_0(D;\mathbb R^d),\qquad Q_h=S^1_h\cap L^2_0(D).$$

For the conforming mini-element spaces $V_h,Q_h$, define the **weak discrete divergence kernel** by
$$Z_h:=\{v_h\in V_h:b(v_h,q_h)=0\text{ for every }q_h\in Q_h\},$$
and the **exact discrete divergence kernel** by
$$Z_h^0:=\{v_h\in V_h:\operatorname{div}v_h=0\text{ almost everywhere on }D\}.$$

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $f:\Omega\to X$ be strongly measurable. Then $f$ is Bochner integrable if
and only if

$$\int_\Omega\|f\|\,d\mu<\infty.$$

Here an a.e.-defined scalar function is integrated through any measurable
representative supplied by the strong simple approximation. Moreover the
Bochner integral is independent of the approximating sequence in its
definition.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and $X$ a real or complex
Banach space. A strongly measurable function $f:\Omega\to X$ is
**Bochner integrable** if there is a sequence of integrable $X$-valued simple
functions $(s_n)$ such that

$$\lim_{n\to\infty}\int_\Omega\|f-s_n\|\,d\mu=0.$$

For such a sequence define

$$\int_\Omega f\,d\mu:=\lim_{n\to\infty}\int_\Omega s_n\,d\mu.$$

The displayed norm limit exists: the simple integral inequality gives

$$\left\|\int s_n-\int s_m\right\|\leq\int\|s_n-s_m\|\leq\int\|s_n-f\|+\int\|f-s_m\|,$$

so the simple integrals form a Cauchy sequence, and $X$ is complete. The next
theorem proves that the value is independent of the approximating sequence and
characterizes existence by integrability of $\|f\|$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $p,q\in[1,\infty]$ be
conjugate exponents, and let $f,g$ be measurable real-valued functions.

1. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $q<\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^q(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_p\|g\|_q.$$
2. If $p=1$ and $q=\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$ and
   $g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_1\|g\|_\infty.$$

   $g\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\|g\|_1.$$

Let $\psi_{z,F_z}\in P_1(F_z)$ be the unique dual affine function satisfying $\int_{F_z}\psi_{z,F_z}\varphi_y=\delta_{zy}$ for the facet's P1 nodal basis. Define
$$I_hv=\sum_z\left(\int_{F_z}\psi_{z,F_z}\operatorname{tr}v\right)\varphi_z.$$

$$\|v-I_hv\|_{L^2(K)}\le Ch_K\|\nabla v\|_{L^2(\omega_K)}.$$

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, let $k\in\mathbb N_0$, let $1\le p\le\infty$, and let
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$.

Every $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ belongs to
$W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$. Indeed $\varphi$ is bounded with compact support,
hence lies in $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ for every exponent in range, and each of
its classical partial derivatives is again smooth and compactly supported,
hence lies in $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and is the corresponding weak derivative
by [[lem-classical-derivatives-are-weak-derivatives]].

Define the **zero-boundary Sobolev space**
$$W_0^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K):=\overline{C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)},$$
the closure taken in the normed space
$(W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K),\|\cdot\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)})$ of
[[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]. The norm is a genuine norm on classes
by [[lem-sobolev-norm-is-well-defined-and-definite]], so this is the usual
metric closure of a subset of a normed space: $u\in W_0^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$
if and only if for every $\delta>0$ there is
$\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with
$\|u-\varphi\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}<\delta$. Write
$H_0^k(\Omega):=W_0^{k,2}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ when the scalar field is fixed by
context.

Three warnings are part of the definition. First, this is a closure of
almost-everywhere classes, and all its equalities are equalities of Sobolev
classes. Second, no pointwise boundary values and no trace characterization
are asserted: a description of $W_0^{k,p}$ by vanishing boundary data belongs
to the later trace theory and is not used here. Third, the closure is defined
for every $1\le p\le\infty$, but for $p=\infty$ it is not claimed that every
compactly supported $W^{k,\infty}(\Omega)$ function lies in $W_0^{k,\infty}(\Omega)$;
the definition merely names the closure of the test functions.

If $v\in V_\sigma$, then $b(v,q_h)=0$ for all $q_h\in Q_h$ by definition of $V_\sigma$ and $b$. Preservation [F4] gives $b(\Pi_hv,q_h)=0$ for every $q_h$, so $\Pi_hv\in Z_h$.

Let $v\in C_c^\infty(D)^d$ and extend it by zero to $\mathbb R^d$. On each cell $K$, choose a vertex $x_K$ and let $p_K$ be the affine Taylor polynomial of $v$ there. Every selected facet used in $I_h$ for a vertex of $K$ lies within $Ch_K$ of $x_K$ by the patch geometry in the face-average interpolation supplier. Apply [F6] on the convex open set $\mathbb R^d$; the pointwise Taylor error on those facets is at most $Ch_K^2\|D^2v\|_\infty$. The scaled dual moments in [F5] then bound the coefficients of $I_h(v-p_K)$ on $K$ by the same amount. Since $I_h$ reproduces $p_K$, this yields $\|v-I_hv\|_{L^\infty(K)}\le Ch_K^2\|D^2v\|_\infty$ and $|c_K|\le Ch_K^2\|D^2v\|_\infty$. Bubble scaling [F3] gives $\|\nabla(b_Kc_K)\|_{L^2(K)}\le Ch_K^{d/2+1}\|D^2v\|_\infty$. Also $h_K^d\le C|K|$ by [F3], so summing squares gives $\|\nabla(\Pi_hv-I_hv)\|_2\le Ch\|D^2v\|_\infty$. The H2-to-H1 estimate in [F5] gives $\|I_hv-v\|_V\to0$, hence $\Pi_hv\to v$ in $V$.

On each cell, $v-\Pi_hv=e_K-b_Kc_K$, so step 1.1 and the triangle inequality give $\|v-\Pi_hv\|_{L^2(K)}\le C\|v-I_hv\|_{L^2(K)}$. Square, sum over cells, apply [F2], and use bounded patch overlap to obtain $\|v-\Pi_hv\|_{L^2(D)}\le Ch\|\nabla v\|_{L^2(D)}$.

For general $v\in V$, choose $\phi\in C_c^\infty(D)^d$ with $\|v-\phi\|_V<\epsilon$, using [F7]. Uniform Fortin stability [F7] gives $\|\Pi_hv-v\|_V\le(C_F+1)\epsilon+\|\Pi_h\phi-\phi\|_V$. Let $h\to0$ by step 1.3 and then $\epsilon\downarrow0$. This proves strong $H^1_0$ convergence for every fixed $v$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

For a partition $0=t_0<\cdots<t_N=T$, write $\tau_n=t_n-t_{n-1}$ and $f_h^n=\tau_n^{-1}\int_{t_{n-1}}^{t_n}f(t)\,dt$. Assume Countable Choice. Let $D\subset\mathbb R^d$, $d=2$ or $3$, be a bounded connected Lipschitz polygonal/polyhedral domain with a conforming shape-regular affine simplicial mesh $\mathcal T_h$. On a simplex $K$ with barycentric coordinates $\lambda_0,\ldots,\lambda_d$, define the scalar interior bubble $b_K=(d+1)^{d+1}\prod_{i=0}^d\lambda_i$. Let
$$S^1_h=\{w\in C^0(\overline D):w|_K\in P_1(K)\},\quad S^1_{h,0}=S^1_h\cap H^1_0(D).$$
The **mini-element spaces** are
$$V_h=[S^1_{h,0}]^d\oplus\bigoplus_{K\in\mathcal T_h}b_K\mathbb R^d\subset H^1_0(D;\mathbb R^d),\qquad Q_h=S^1_h\cap L^2_0(D).$$
Each bubble is extended by zero off its cell. The zero-boundary conformity of the piecewise affine part is supplied by [[thm-zero-boundary-piecewise-polynomials-in-w10p]]. The local/global dimensions are proved in the next dimension lemma.

For the conforming mini-element spaces $V_h,Q_h$, define the **weak discrete divergence kernel** by
$$Z_h:=\{v_h\in V_h:b(v_h,q_h)=0\text{ for every }q_h\in Q_h\},$$
and the **exact discrete divergence kernel** by
$$Z_h^0:=\{v_h\in V_h:\operatorname{div}v_h=0\text{ almost everywhere on }D\}.$$
Since $b(v_h,q_h)=-\int_Dq_h\operatorname{div}v_h$, one has $Z_h^0\subseteq Z_h$. Equality is not part of either definition; the companion example proves strictness for a concrete mesh.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice.

Let $1 \le p < \infty$. The finite linear combinations of indicator functions of
half-open boxes with rational endpoints and rational coefficients form a
countable dense subset of $L^p(\mathbb{R}^n)$.

A topological space $X$ is **separable** if some at most countable subset $D\subseteq X$ is dense in $X$ ([[def-dense-top]], [[def-countable]]). Equivalently, every nonempty open subset of $X$ meets $D$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $M$ be a closed linear subspace of a real or complex Hilbert space $H$. Then every $x\in H$ has a unique decomposition

$$x=m+n,\qquad m\in M,\quad n\in M^\perp ,$$

so that $H=M\oplus M^\perp$ as a direct sum of the subspace $M$ and its orthogonal complement.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $0<T<\infty$, let $H$ be a separable real Hilbert space, let $X\subseteq H$ be a dense real linear subspace, and let $u_0\in H$. Suppose $u\in L^2(0,T;H)$ and $\|u(t)\|_H\le M$ for almost every $t$, for some finite $M$. Suppose also that for every $v\in X$ there is $h_v\in L^1(0,T)$ such that, for every $\eta\in C^1([0,T])$ vanishing near $T$,
$$-\int_0^T (u(t),v)_H\eta'(t)\,dt=\int_0^T h_v(t)\eta(t)\,dt+(u_0,v)_H\eta(0).$$
Then there is a unique weakly continuous map $\widetilde u:[0,T]\to H$ equal to $u$ almost everywhere and satisfying $\widetilde u(0)=u_0$. Here weak continuity means that $t\mapsto(\widetilde u(t),w)_H$ is continuous for every $w\in H$.

derivations.claim: Since $u_0\in H_\sigma=\overline{V_\sigma}^{L^2}$, for any $\epsilon>0$ choose $v\in V_\sigma$ with $\|u_0-v\|_2<\epsilon$. By [F3], $\Pi_jv\in Z_j$ and $\|\Pi_jv-v\|_2\to0$. The best-approximation property [F4] gives $\|P_{Z_j}u_0-u_0\|_2\le\|\Pi_jv-u_0\|_2\le\|\Pi_jv-v\|_2+\epsilon$. Letting $j\to\infty$ and then $\epsilon\downarrow0$ proves strong convergence of the discrete initial data.
Apply [F1] to every mesh and partition. The energy inequality gives uniform bounds for $\max_n\|u_j^n\|_2$ and $\|\overline u_j\|_{L^2V}$; it also gives $\|\overline u_j\|_{L^\infty H}\le M$.

Fix a finite orthonormal family $e_1,\ldots,e_m\in V_\sigma$. For each mesh, $\Pi_je_i\in Z_j$ by [F3], so testing the discrete equation [F13] with $\Pi_je_i$ removes pressure. The backward difference of $a_{j,i}^n=(u_j^n,\Pi_je_i)_2$ is therefore bounded by $|(D_\tau a_{j,i}^n)|\le C_{e_i}\big(\|f_j^n\|_2+\nu\|u_j^n\|_V+\|u_j^n\|_2^{1/2}\|u_j^n\|_V^{3/2}\big).$ The first two terms are bounded in $L^2(0,T)$ by [F1], and the last in $L^{4/3}(0,T)$ by [F11], because its $4/3$ power is at most $M^{2/3}C\|u_j^n\|_V^2$. Thus the coefficient condition of [F2] holds for every finite family.

By [F2], after a subsequence $\overline u_j\to u$ strongly in $L^2(0,T;L^2)$. The energy bounds [F1] and [F9] give, after a further subsequence, $\overline u_j\rightharpoonup u$ in $L^2(0,T;V)$. Apply [F10] to the scalar functions $t\mapsto\|\overline u_j(t)-u(t)\|_2$ to obtain almost-everywhere-in-time strong convergence along a further subsequence. The uniform $L^\infty H$ bound then implies $u\in L^\infty(0,T;H)$.

For any $q\in C_c^\infty(D)$, apply the face-average interpolant to $q-|D|^{-1}\int_Dq$ and subtract the mean of its interpolant to obtain $q_j\in Q_j$ converging in $L^2$, using the approximation estimate in [[lem-na-scott-zhang-boundary-preserving-p1-interpolant]]. Since $b(u_j^n,q_j)=0$, [F6] gives $\int_Dq\,\operatorname{div}u_j^n=0$ for the $q_j$ part and $\int_D\operatorname{div}u_j^n=0$ for the mean part. The $L^2$ approximation error times the uniformly bounded $L^2(0,T;V)$ divergence norm tends to zero by Holder. Passing to the weak gradient limit proves $\operatorname{div}u=0$ a.e.; hence $u\in L^2(0,T;V_\sigma)$.

Let $v\in V_\sigma$ and $\eta\in C^1([0,T])$ vanish near $T$. Test each time step [F13] by $\Pi_jv\in Z_j$, multiply by the left-endpoint value $\eta(t_{n-1}^j)$, and sum. Discrete summation by parts gives $-(u_j^0,\Pi_jv)_2\eta(0)-\sum_{n=1}^{N_j-1}(u_j^n,\Pi_jv)_2(\eta(t_n^j)-\eta(t_{n-1}^j))$; the terminal term is zero for all fine partitions because $\eta$ vanishes near $T$. The sum is exactly the integral of $-\overline u_j\cdot\Pi_jv\,\eta'$ on the nonterminal cells, so the time contribution converges to $-(u_0,v)_2\eta(0)-\int_0^T(u,v)_2\eta'$. Moving its initial term to the right side gives the required positive initial trace. Uniform convergence of the left-endpoint step approximation to $\eta$, [F3], and step 1.1 justify these limits. The viscosity term converges by weak $L^2V$ convergence and $\Pi_jv\to v$ in $V$; the force averages converge by [F7] and the same uniform time-test approximation.

For almost every $t$, choose the first time node $t_j(t)\ge t$ and sum the work-form energy inequality of [F1] through that node. Then $\overline u_j(t)=u_j^{n_j(t)}$, so step 1.4 gives the required strong convergence of the kinetic-energy term for almost every $t$. By [F7], $f_j\to f$ in $L^2H$ and $\overline u_j\to u$ in $L^2H$, so their work integrals converge on $[0,t]$. The overshoot interval $[t,t_j(t)]$ contributes at most $\|f_j\|_{L^2H}M\sqrt{\tau_{\max}^j}$ by Cauchy--Schwarz and the uniform $L^\infty H$ bound, hence tends to zero. The gradient sum through $t_j(t)$ is bounded below by its integral through $t$; weak $L^2V$ convergence and [F9] give lower semicontinuity on $[0,t]$. The initial projections converge by step 1.1. This proves the energy inequality for almost every $t$.

The test interpolation error in convection vanishes: continuity from [F11] bounds its integral by $C\|\Pi_jv-v\|_V\|\overline u_j\|_{L^2V}^2\|\eta\|_\infty$. The uniform left-endpoint test approximation from step 2.2 permits replacing the discrete weights by $\eta$. For fixed $v\in V_\sigma$, strong $L^2L^2$ convergence and the uniform $L^2L^6$ bound imply strong $L^2L^3$ and strong $L^2L^4$ convergence of velocities by Holder interpolation. In the skew formula, $u_j\otimes v$ then converges strongly in $L^2L^2$ while $\nabla u_j$ converges weakly in $L^2L^2$; $u_j\otimes u_j$ converges strongly in $L^1L^2$. Thus the convective term passes to $c(u;u,v)$. This proves the limiting momentum equation for all solenoidal tests.

By [F14], $L^2(D)^d$ is separable, so balls with centers in a countable dense set and positive rational radii form a countable base. The space $H_\sigma=\overline{V_\sigma}^{L^2}$ from [F12] is a closed subspace and hence Hilbert by [F14]; intersecting that countable base with $H_\sigma$ gives a countable base there, and [A1] selects one point from each nonempty member to make a dense set. For every $v\in V_\sigma$, steps 2.2 and 3.1 give the scalar weak equation with $h_v(t)=(f(t),v)_{L^2}-a_\nu(u(t),v)-c(u(t);u(t),v)$. This function is integrable: its three terms lie in $L^2(0,T)$, $L^2(0,T)$, and $L^{4/3}(0,T)$ respectively by the data, energy bound [F1], and convection bound [F11]; finite $T$ embeds these spaces into $L^1$. The uniform $L^\infty H$ bound follows from step 1.4. Apply [F15] with $H=H_\sigma$ and $X=V_\sigma$ to obtain a unique weakly continuous representative with initial value $u_0$. Its energy inequality is already proved in step 2.3.

Steps 1.4, 2.1–2.3, 3.1, and 4.1 give the strong and weak convergence, divergence constraint, solenoidal momentum equation, weakly continuous initial trace, and energy inequality required by [[def-na-solenoidal-energy-weak-ns-velocity]]. The stronger pressure-bearing PE06 claim is not inferred here and remains escalated as stated.

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) at which $g$ is differentiable
([[def-derivative]]), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the

([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$

derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and

there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $\psi_{z,F_z}\in P_1(F_z)$ be the unique dual affine function satisfying $\int_{F_z}\psi_{z,F_z}\varphi_y=\delta_{zy}$ for the facet's P1 nodal basis. Define
$$I_hv=\sum_z\left(\int_{F_z}\psi_{z,F_z}\operatorname{tr}v\right)\varphi_z.$$
This is a linear face-average interpolant $H^1(D)\to S_h$, where $S_h$ is the continuous piecewise P1 space. It maps $H^1_0(D)$ into $S_h\cap H^1_0(D)$, is uniformly $H^1$-seminorm stable, and for each element patch $\omega_K$ has
$$\|v-I_hv\|_{L^2(K)}\le Ch_K\|\nabla v\|_{L^2(\omega_K)}.$$
If $v\in H^2(D)$, then $\|\nabla(v-I_hv)\|_{L^2(K)}\le Ch_K\|D^2v\|_{L^2(\omega_K)}$. Constants depend only on dimension, the fixed domain, and the mesh shape-regularity bound. No point evaluation is used.

$$S^1_h=\{w\in C^0(\overline D):w|_K\in P_1(K)\},\quad S^1_{h,0}=S^1_h\cap H^1_0(D).$$
The **mini-element spaces** are
$$V_h=[S^1_{h,0}]^d\oplus\bigoplus_{K\in\mathcal T_h}b_K\mathbb R^d\subset H^1_0(D;\mathbb R^d),\qquad Q_h=S^1_h\cap L^2_0(D).$$
Each bubble is extended by zero off its cell. The zero-boundary conformity of the piecewise affine part is supplied by [[thm-zero-boundary-piecewise-polynomials-in-w10p]]. The local/global dimensions are proved in the next dimension lemma.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $p,q\in[1,\infty]$ be
conjugate exponents, and let $f,g$ be measurable real-valued functions.

1. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $q<\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^q(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_p\|g\|_q.$$
2. If $p=1$ and $q=\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$ and
   $g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_1\|g\|_\infty.$$
3. If $p=\infty$ and $q=1$ with $f\in L^\infty(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\|g\|_1.$$

In every case the right-hand side is finite, so $fg$ is integrable.

$$uv\le\frac{u^p}{p}+\frac{v^q}{q}.$$

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

$$a(u,v)+b(v,p)=F(v),\qquad b(u,q)=G(q)$$

The functions $\sin$ and $\cos$ are differentiable on $\mathbb R$, with
$$(\sin x)'=\cos x,\qquad(\cos x)'=-\sin x.$$
Also $\sin0=0$ and $\cos0=1$.

For every real $x$,
$$\sin(2x)=2\sin x\cos x,\quad \cos(2x)=\cos^2x-\sin^2x=2\cos^2x-1=1-2\sin^2x,$$
and
$$\sin^2x=(1-\cos2x)/2,\qquad \cos^2x=(1+\cos2x)/2.$$
When defined, $\tan(2x)=2\tan x/(1-\tan^2x)$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[thm-sine-and-cosine-addition-formulas]], [[cor-trigonometric-parity-and-pythagorean-identity]], [[def-tangent-cotangent-secant-cosecant]].

For every real $x$,
$$\sin x=0\Longleftrightarrow x=m\pi\text{ for some }m\in\mathbb Z,\qquad \cos x=0\Longleftrightarrow x=(m+1/2)\pi\text{ for some }m\in\mathbb Z.$$
Both sine and cosine have period $2\pi$, and no smaller positive number is a common period.

In particular $(\exp)'=\exp$.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be integrable
([[def-darboux-integral]]), let $F$ be its integral function
([[def-the-integral-function]]), and let $c \in [a,b]$ be a point at which $f$ is
continuous ([[def-continuity-real]]). Then $F$ is differentiable at $c$ as a
function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]) and

$$F'(c) \;=\; f(c) .$$

At $c = a$ and $c = b$ this is the one-sided statement, which is what
[[def-derivative]] means at those points: every point of a nondegenerate interval
is a limit point of it, so $F'(c)$ is a meaningful symbol at every $c \in [a,b]$,

primitive of $f$ there**: $F' = f$ at every point of $[a,b]$.

differ from $f(c)$; both are exhibited on the companion page, by
an integrable function with no primitive and by a false
statement about the integral function.

Fix an integer $d\ge2$. The **reference open simplex** is
$$\widehat S_d:=\{\widehat x\in\mathbb R^d:\widehat x_i>0\ (1\le i\le d),\ \sum_{i=1}^d\widehat x_i<1\},$$
with closure $\overline{\widehat S_d}=\operatorname{conv}\{0,e_1,\ldots,e_d\}$.

A **matching affine simplicial mesh** of a bounded polyhedral open set
$\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d$ is a finite set $\mathcal T$ of closed,
nondegenerate $d$-simplices such that their union is $\overline\Omega$,
their interiors are pairwise disjoint, $\Omega$ is the interior of their
union, and the intersection of two distinct cells is either empty or a
whole face of each. Thus no lower-dimensional crack is omitted from
$\Omega$ while its surrounding cells are retained. Every interior facet is
incident to exactly two cells and every boundary facet to one. The faces of
a cell are the convex hulls of its vertex subsets. A facet means a face of
dimension $d-1$.

For each cell $K\in\mathcal T$, an affine bijection
$$F_K:\overline{\widehat S_d}\to K,\qquad F_K(\widehat x)=b_K+A_K\widehat x,$$
with invertible $A_K\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}$ is a **reference map**.
Choose the vertex order so $\det A_K>0$; this is the orientation convention
used for Piola formulas. Write $h_K:=\operatorname{diam}(K)$ and let
$\rho_K$ be the radius of the largest Euclidean ball contained in $K$.
A family $\{\mathcal T_h\}_{h\in H}$ is **shape regular** if there is a
finite $\sigma$ such that $h_K/\rho_K\le\sigma$ for every
$h\in H$ and $K\in\mathcal T_h$. This universal condition is vacuous for
an empty family.
This definition uses radius; references using the diameter of the inscribed
ball differ by a factor of two.

An affine image of the reference square is a parallelogram. A general
quadrilateral requires a nonaffine map and is outside this affine definition;
curved-cell approximation is not included here.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $F_K(\widehat x)=b_K+A_K\widehat x$ map the fixed reference simplex

$h_K$ be its diameter and $\rho_K$ its inradius. There are constants
$c,C>0$, depending only on $d$, the reference simplex, and the shape
regularity bound, such that
$$c h_K\le s_{\min}(A_K)\le \|A_K\|\le C h_K, \qquad c h_K^d\le\det A_K\le C h_K^d.$$
For each facet $F$, its affine surface Jacobian is comparable to
$h_K^{d-1}$, and its altitude from the opposite vertex is comparable to
$h_K$. Thus Sobolev scaling constants can be expressed using $h_K$ alone,
with constants uniform over the family.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

In ZF, assume the Axiom of Choice. Then the Axiom of Countable Choice holds.
Moreover, if $R\subseteq X\times X$ is a serial relation on a nonempty set
$X$ and $a\in X$, there is a sequence $(x_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ such that
$x_0=a$ and $x_nRx_{n+1}$ for every $n$. Thus AC supplies the
prescribed-initial-point form of Dependent Choice.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice as inherited from [[def-na-evolutionary-incompressible-ns-weak-solution]]. Let $D$, $V$, $Q$, $V_\sigma$, $H_\sigma$, $a_\nu$, and $c$ be as in [[def-na-evolutionary-incompressible-ns-weak-solution]]; the Stokes velocity and pressure spaces are $V=H^1_0(D)^d$ and $Q=L^2_0(D)$ as specified in [[def-na-stokes-zero-mean-pressure-and-velocity-spaces]]. For $f\in L^2(0,T;L^2(D)^d)$ and $u_0\in H_\sigma$, a **solenoidal energy weak velocity** is a velocity $u\in L^\infty(0,T;H_\sigma)\cap L^2(0,T;V_\sigma)$ that is weakly continuous into $H_\sigma$, satisfies $\operatorname{div}u=0$ almost everywhere, and obeys the scalar-test weak equation
$$-\int_0^T(u(t),v)_{L^2}\eta'(t)\,dt+\int_0^T\big(a_\nu(u(t),v)+c(u(t);u(t),v)\big)\eta(t)\,dt=\int_0^T(f(t),v)_{L^2}\eta(t)\,dt+(u_0,v)_{L^2}\eta(0)$$
for every fixed $v\in V_\sigma$ and $\eta\in C^1([0,T])$ vanishing near $T$. It also satisfies, for almost every $t\in(0,T)$,
$$\frac12\|u(t)\|_{L^2}^2+\nu\int_0^t\|\nabla u(s)\|_{L^2}^2\,ds\le\frac12\|u_0\|_{L^2}^2+\int_0^t(f(s),u(s))_{L^2}\,ds.$$
This solenoidal definition does not itself assert a pressure exists in $L^{4/3}(0,T;L^2_0(D))$; that is a separate regularity conclusion.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $D\subset\mathbb R^d$ be bounded and open. If $v\in H^1_0(D;\mathbb R^d)$, then $\operatorname{div}v\in L^2(D)$ and $\int_D\operatorname{div}v=0$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, $n\ge2$, $1\le p<n$ and $p^{*}=\frac{np}{n-p}$. There is $C(n,p)$ with
$$\|u\|_{L^{p^{*}}(\Omega)}\le C(n,p)\|Du\|_{L^p(\Omega)}$$
for every $u\in W^{1,p}_0(\Omega;\mathbb K)$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $p,q\in[1,\infty]$ be
conjugate exponents, and let $f,g$ be measurable real-valued functions.

1. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $q<\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^q(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_p\|g\|_q.$$
2. If $p=1$ and $q=\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$ and
   $g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_1\|g\|_\infty.$$
3. If $p=\infty$ and $q=1$ with $f\in L^\infty(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\|g\|_1.$$

In every case the right-hand side is finite, so $fg$ is integrable.

Let $D\subset\mathbb R^d$ be nonempty, bounded, connected and Lipschitz, with $d\in\{2,3\}$. Under Countable Choice there is a bounded linear map $B_D:L^2_0(D)\to H^1_0(D;\mathbb R^d)$ such that
$$\operatorname{div}B_Dq=q,\qquad \|\nabla B_Dq\|_2\le C_{\rm div}(D)\|q\|_2.$$
For a chosen finite cover and tree decomposition from [[lem-na-lipschitz-domain-finite-star-shaped-cover]] and [[lem-na-finite-cover-zero-mean-data-decomposition]], one valid bound is $C_{\rm div}(D)=\sum_i C_{U_i}D_i$; it is finite and independent of any finite-element mesh.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and $X$ a real or complex
Banach space. A strongly measurable function $f:\Omega\to X$ is
**Bochner integrable** if there is a sequence of integrable $X$-valued simple
functions $(s_n)$ such that

$$\lim_{n\to\infty}\int_\Omega\|f-s_n\|\,d\mu=0.$$

For such a sequence define

$$\int_\Omega f\,d\mu:=\lim_{n\to\infty}\int_\Omega s_n\,d\mu.$$

The displayed norm limit exists: the simple integral inequality gives

$$\left\|\int s_n-\int s_m\right\|\leq\int\|s_n-s_m\|\leq\int\|s_n-f\|+\int\|f-s_m\|,$$

so the simple integrals form a Cauchy sequence, and $X$ is complete. The next
theorem proves that the value is independent of the approximating sequence and
characterizes existence by integrability of $\|f\|$.

For $E\in\mathcal A$, write
$\int_Ef\,d\mu:=\int_\Omega\mathbf1_Ef\,d\mu$ whenever this function is
Bochner integrable.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and $X$ a real or complex
Banach space. A function $f:\Omega\to X$ is **strongly measurable** (or
**Bochner measurable**) if there are measurable $X$-valued simple functions
$s_n$ and a measurable null set $N$ such that

$$\lim_{n\to\infty}\|s_n(\omega)-f(\omega)\|=0$$

for every $\omega\in\Omega\setminus N$.

This is a norm-convergence condition. It is not, by definition, merely Borel
measurability of $f$ or measurability of every scalar function $x^*\circ f$.
Changing $f$ on a null set preserves strong measurability: enlarge $N$ by that
null set and retain the same approximants.

Let $f:\Omega\to X$ be strongly measurable. Then $f$ is Bochner integrable if
and only if

$$\int_\Omega\|f\|\,d\mu<\infty.$$

Here an a.e.-defined scalar function is integrated through any measurable
representative supplied by the strong simple approximation. Moreover the
Bochner integral is independent of the approximating sequence in its
definition.

If $f:\Omega\to X$ is Bochner integrable, then for every measurable $E$,

$$\left\|\int_E f\,d\mu\right\|\leq\int_E\|f\|\,d\mu.$$

Let $X,Y$ be Banach spaces, let $T:X\to Y$ be bounded and linear, and let $f$
be Bochner integrable. Then $T\circ f$ is Bochner integrable and, for every
measurable $E$,

$$T\left(\int_Ef\,d\mu\right)=\int_E Tf\,d\mu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice for the ACL and absolutely-continuous
fundamental-theorem interfaces. Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open
interval, let $1\le p\le\infty$, let $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$,
and let $u\in W^{1,p}(I;\mathbb K)$, with weak derivative class $Du$. Then
there is exactly one continuous representative $u^*$ of the class of $u$ on
$I$ that is locally absolutely continuous, that is, absolutely continuous on
every compact interval contained in $I$, and satisfies
$$u^*(x)-u^*(y)=\int_y^xDu(t)\,dt\qquad\text{for every }x,y\in I,$$
where for $x<y$ the right-hand side denotes $-\int_x^yDu$, equivalently
$u^*(y)-u^*(x)=\int_x^yDu$ whenever $x\le y$.

If $I=(a,b)$ has finite endpoints, then $Du\in L^1(a,b)$, the representative
$u^*$ extends uniquely to an absolutely continuous function on $[a,b]$, and
the extension satisfies
$$u^*(x)=u^*(a)+\int_a^xDu(t)\,dt\qquad\text{for every }x\in[a,b].$$

The scalar field is arbitrary, $p=1$ and $p=\infty$ are included, and the
one-dimensional interval may be bounded or unbounded. The Axiom of Choice is
used only through the Countable-Choice and Dependent-Choice hypotheses of the
cited characterisation, fundamental-theorem and completeness interfaces.

Assume the Axioms of Countable Choice and Dependent Choice. For $F:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$, the following are equivalent:

1. $F$ is absolutely continuous.
2. $F'$ exists almost everywhere, $F'\in L^1[a,b]$, and
$$F(x)-F(a)=\int_a^xF'(t)\,dt\quad\text{for every }x\in[a,b].$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. The map $f\mapsto u_f$, $u_f(\varphi)=\int_\Omega f\varphi$, is a complex-linear injection from $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$ modulo almost-everywhere equality into $\mathcal D'(\Omega)$. It is continuous from the local $L^1$ topology, generated by $f\mapsto\int_K|f|$ for compact $K\subseteq\Omega$, to the strong distribution topology. In particular local $L^1$ convergence implies strong distribution convergence. The continuity estimate itself is choice-free; Countable Choice is used in the cited $L^1$ approximate-identity theorem proving injectivity.

For a distribution $u\in\mathcal D'(\Omega)$ in the convention of [[def-distribution]] and a multi-index $\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n$, its **distributional derivative** is
$$\langle\partial^\alpha u,\varphi\rangle=(-1)^{|\alpha|}\langle u,\partial^\alpha\varphi\rangle\qquad(\varphi\in\mathcal D(\Omega)).$$
The test derivative is a continuous linear endomorphism by [[thm-test-function-operations-are-continuous]]. Its composition with $u$, multiplied by the indicated sign, is therefore a continuous complex-linear functional, so this definition produces a distribution. The pairing is bilinear, with no complex conjugation. For $\alpha=0$ the operation is the identity; for one coordinate derivative its sign is minus. Every derivative of the zero distribution is zero, including on the empty domain. No choice axiom enters this construction. Compatibility with classical derivatives requires an integration-by-parts argument where it is used; it is not part of the definition.

**Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice** ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$(A_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a sequence of subsets of $\mathbb{R}$, each of
measure zero ([[def-measure-zero-and-content-zero]]). Then

$$\bigcup_{n \in \mathbb{N}} A_n \quad \text{has measure zero.}$$

By the padding convention of [[def-measure-zero-and-content-zero]] and
[[def-countable]] the same conclusion covers the union of an at most countable
family of null sets, a finite family being extended by copies of $\varnothing$.

**The hypothesis $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ is spent at exactly one step, step 2.1
below**, where one covering sequence is selected for every $A_n$ at once. Each
$A_n$ has many such covers and nullity provides no rule for singling one out.
Nothing else in the proof selects anything: the diagonal enumeration and the
estimate are formulas.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let
$L^2(\mu)$ be the quotient of $\mathcal L^2(\mu)$ by the almost-everywhere zero
functions ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]), with the quotient
norm $\|\cdot\|_2$ ([[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]]).

1. On **real** $L^2(\mu)$ the formula
   $$\langle f,g\rangle:=\int fg\,d\mu$$is a well-defined inner product, linear in both variables, positive definite, with $\langle f,f\rangle=\|f\|_2^2$; with it $L^2(\mu)$ is a real Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]). 2. On **complex** $L^2(\mu;\mathbb C)$ the formula$$\langle f,g\rangle:=\int f\overline g\,d\mu$$
   is a well-defined inner product, linear in the first variable and
   conjugate-linear in the second, positive definite, with
   $\langle f,f\rangle=\|f\|_2^2$; with it $L^2(\mu;\mathbb C)$ is a complex
   Hilbert space ([[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]).

In both cases the inner product induces exactly the established quotient
$L^2$ norm.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice.

Let $1 \le p < \infty$. The finite linear combinations of indicator functions of
half-open boxes with rational endpoints and rational coefficients form a
countable dense subset of $L^p(\mathbb{R}^n)$.

A topological space $X$ is **separable** if some at most countable subset $D\subseteq X$ is dense in $X$ ([[def-dense-top]], [[def-countable]]). Equivalently, every nonempty open subset of $X$ meets $D$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $M$ be a closed linear subspace of a real or complex Hilbert space $H$. Then every $x\in H$ has a unique decomposition

$$x=m+n,\qquad m\in M,\quad n\in M^\perp ,$$

so that $H=M\oplus M^\perp$ as a direct sum of the subspace $M$ and its orthogonal complement.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $H$ be a real or complex Hilbert space and let $f$ be a bounded linear functional on $H$ ([[def-dual-space-of-a-normed-space]]). Then there is a unique $y\in H$ with

$$f(x)=\langle x,y\rangle\qquad\text{for every }x\in H,$$

and $\|f\|=\|y\|$, where $\|f\|$ is the dual norm ([[def-operator-norm]]). Under the first-variable-linear convention the representing vector depends conjugate-linearly and isometrically on $f$: if $f_i$ is represented by $y_i$ and $a,b$ are scalars, then $af_1+bf_2$ is represented by $\overline a\,y_1+\overline b\,y_2$.

Assume Countable Choice. Every bounded sequence in a separable real Hilbert
space $X$ has a weakly convergent subsequence. If $V$ is a separable real
Hilbert space, then $L^2(0,T;V)$ and $L^2(0,T;V^*)$ are separable real Hilbert
spaces, their product is a separable Hilbert space, and the graph of the weak
time-derivative operator is closed there. Consequently $W(0,T;V)$ is a closed
Hilbert subspace of that product and every bounded sequence in $W(0,T;V)$ has
a weakly convergent subsequence.

Assume Countable Choice as inherited from the energy-space conventions. Interpret each interval forcing average as a Bochner integral; its existence follows from the stated L2 forcing and the Bochner integrability criterion ([[def-countable-choice]], [[thm-bochner-integrability-criterion]]). Let $D$ be as in [[def-na-evolutionary-incompressible-ns-weak-solution]], let $\mathcal T_h$ be a conforming shape-regular affine simplicial mesh of $D$, and let $V_h,Q_h,Z_h$ be the MINI spaces and weak divergence kernel of [[def-na-mini-element-p1-bubble-p1-spaces]] and [[def-na-discrete-weak-and-exact-divergence-free-spaces]]. For a partition $0=t_0<\cdots<t_N=T$, write $\tau_n=t_n-t_{n-1}$ and $f_h^n=\tau_n^{-1}\int_{t_{n-1}}^{t_n}f(t)\,dt$. Given $u_h^0\in Z_h$, a **backward Euler mini-element solution** is a sequence $(u_h^n,p_h^n)\in V_h\times Q_h$ satisfying, for $n=1,\ldots,N$,
$$\left(\frac{u_h^n-u_h^{n-1}}{\tau_n},v_h\right)_{L^2}+a_\nu(u_h^n,v_h)+c(u_h^n;u_h^n,v_h)+b(v_h,p_h^n)=(f_h^n,v_h)_{L^2}\quad(v_h\in V_h),$$
$$b(u_h^n,q_h)=0\quad(q_h\in Q_h).$$
All pressure variables use the zero-mean gauge $Q_h\subset L^2_0(D)$. Restriction to $v_h\in Z_h$ eliminates pressure. The equations are well-defined by [[lem-na-mini-be-scheme-is-well-defined]]; this definition claims no solver termination or error rate.

Assume Countable Choice, the mini-element hypotheses of [[def-na-mini-navier-stokes-backward-euler-scheme]], $f\in L^2(0,T;L^2(D)^d)$, and an initial value $u_h^0\in Z_h$. On every finite positive time partition there is at least one mixed solution $(u_h^n,p_h^n)_{n=1}^N$ of the backward Euler scheme. Every such solution satisfies, for $0\le m\le N$, the work-form inequality
$$ rac12\|u_h^m\|_2^2+ rac12\sum_{n=1}^m\|u_h^n-u_h^{n-1}\|_2^2+
u\sum_{n=1}^m	au_n\|
abla u_h^n\|_2^2\le rac12\|u_h^0\|_2^2+\sum_{n=1}^m	au_n(f_h^n,u_h^n)_{L^2}.$$
Consequently it satisfies the mesh-independent estimate
$$ rac12\|u_h^m\|_2^2+ rac12\sum_{n=1}^m\|u_h^n-u_h^{n-1}\|_2^2+ rac{
u}{2}\sum_{n=1}^m	au_n\|
abla u_h^n\|_2^2\le rac12\|u_h^0\|_2^2+ rac{C_P(D)^2}{2
u}\|f\|_{L^2(0,T;L^2)}^2.$$
The constant is independent of mesh size and time-step sizes.

On the mini-element spaces of [[def-na-mini-element-p1-bubble-p1-spaces]], there is a Fortin operator $\Pi_h:V\to V_h$ preserving $b(v,q_h)$ for every $q_h\in Q_h$, with $\|\Pi_hv\|_V\le C_F\|v\|_V$. The constant depends only on $d$ and the mesh shape-regularity bound, not on $h$. Consequently
$$\beta_h\ge (C_FC_{\rm div}(D))^{-1}.$$

Let $\Pi_h:H^1_0(D;\mathbb R^d)\to V_h$ be the MINI Fortin map constructed in [[thm-na-mini-element-fortin-stability]]. On every shape-regular matching mesh, there is a constant $C$ independent of $h$ such that
$$\|v-\Pi_hv\|_{L^2(D)}\le Ch\|\nabla v\|_{L^2(D)}\qquad(v\in H^1_0(D;\mathbb R^d)).$$
For every fixed $v\in H^1_0(D)^d$, $\Pi_hv\to v$ in $H^1_0$ as $h\to0$. If $v\in V_\sigma$, exact Fortin preservation also gives $\Pi_hv\in Z_h$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $V_h,Q_h$ be the stable mini-element spaces on a bounded connected Lipschitz polyhedral domain with a conforming mesh, with viscosity $\nu>0$, and let $Z_h=\{v_h:b(v_h,q_h)=0\ \forall q_h\in Q_h\}$. Choose bases of $V_h,Q_h$, let $M$ be the velocity mass matrix, $A$ the Stokes stiffness matrix, and $B$ the constraint matrix with entries $B_{\ell j}=b(\phi_j,\chi_\ell)$. The mass-orthogonal projector onto $Z_h$ is
$$P_M=I-M^{-1}B^T(BM^{-1}B^T)^{-1}B.$$
On the mean-zero pressure coordinates, both the mass pressure Schur matrix $BM^{-1}B^T$ and stiffness pressure Schur matrix $BA^{-1}B^T$ are positive definite. Before imposing the pressure gauge on the full continuous P1 space, the constant pressure is exactly the one-dimensional nullspace of $B^T$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $D\subset\mathbb R^d$, $d\in\{2,3\}$, be nonempty, bounded, connected, Lipschitz and polyhedral, and let $0<T<\infty$. Let $\{\mathcal T_j\}$ be matching shape-regular affine simplicial meshes with $h_j\to0$, and let the time partitions of $[0,T]$ have maximum step tending to zero, with no relation required between the two limits. Let $f\in L^2(0,T;L^2(D)^d)$ and $u_0\in H_\sigma$. On each mesh take $u_j^0=P_{Z_j}u_0$, the $L^2$-orthogonal projection onto the weak MINI kernel, and choose any backward Euler MINI solution from [[thm-na-mini-be-step-existence-energy]]. Then a subsequence of piecewise-constant velocities converges strongly in $L^2(0,T;L^2(D)^d)$ and weakly in $L^2(0,T;H^1_0(D)^d)$ to a velocity $u$ satisfying the solenoidal weak momentum equation, initial trace and energy inequality in [[def-na-solenoidal-energy-weak-ns-velocity]]. This theorem supplies the velocity limit and its energy inequality. It does not assert the pressure regularity and pressure-bearing formulation required by the PE06 plan; the remaining pressure obligation is explicitly escalated on the A page.

Assume Countable Choice.

Let $X$ be a real Banach space, $0<T<\infty$, and $1\le p<\infty$. For
$f\in L^p(0,T;X)$, translations are continuous in $L^p$ on every compact
subinterval of $(0,T)$. Convolution with a scalar smooth approximate identity
therefore converges to $f$ in $L^p$ on such subintervals. If $\mathcal P_k$
are interval partitions of $[0,T]$ with maximum cell length tending to zero,
the piecewise-constant interval averages of $f$ converge to $f$ in
$L^p(0,T;X)$.

Assume Countable Choice and let $D$ be bounded, connected and Lipschitz. If $1<s<\infty$ and $R\in L^s(0,T;V^*)$ satisfies $R(t)(v)=0$ for every $v\in V_\sigma=\ker(\operatorname{div}:V\to L^2_0(D))$ outside one common null set, then there is a unique $p\in L^s(0,T;L^2_0(D))$ such that $R(t)(v)=b(v,p(t))$ for every $v\in V$ almost everywhere. Moreover, $\|p\|_{L^sL^2}\le C_{\rm div}(D)\|R\|_{L^sV^*}$.

derivations.claim: The weakly continuous representative of $u$ obeys $\|u(t)\|_2\le U$ for every $t\in[0,T]$. Indeed, if $\|u(t_0)\|_2>U$, take $w=u(t_0)/\|u(t_0)\|_2\in H_\sigma$. Weak continuity makes $(u(t),w)$ continuous and greater than $U$ on a relative neighborhood of $t_0$ with positive time measure, contradicting the essential bound $U$.

Define $g(t)\in V^*$ by $g(t)(v)=(f(t),v)_2-a_
u(u(t),v)-c(u(t);u(t),v)$. The first two terms are strongly measurable bounded linear images of Bochner functions; the last is a continuous quadratic map $V	o V^*$ by the trilinear bound in [F3], hence is strongly measurable. Poincare and [F3] give $\|g(t)\|_{V^*}\le C_P\|f(t)\|_2+2
u\|u(t)\|_V+C_c\|u(t)\|_2^{1/2}\|u(t)\|_V^{3/2}.$ Holder makes $g\in L^{4/3}(0,T;V^*)\subset L^1(0,T;V^*)$ and yields $\|g\|_{L^1V^*}\le C_P\sqrt T F+2
u\sqrt T E+C_cT^{1/4}U^{1/2}E^{3/2}$.

For a mixed MINI solution define $\widehat u_h$ by affine interpolation of the velocity nodes and let bars denote right-constant reconstructions. On each time cell, $\partial_tP_h=\overline p_h$ and $\partial_t\widehat u_h=D_\tau u_h^n$. Integrating the discrete equation over complete or partial cells gives, for every $t$ and $v_h\in V_h$, $(\widehat u_h(t)-u_h^0,v_h)_2+\int_0^t\bigl(a_\nu(\overline u_h,v_h)+c(\overline u_h;\overline u_h,v_h)\bigr)\,ds+b(v_h,P_h(t))=\int_0^t(f_h,v_h)_2\,ds.$ Because $P_h(t)\in Q_h$, the uniform inf-sup estimate applies. Convexity gives $\|\widehat u_h(t)\|_2\le U_h$; [F2], Holder, and [F3] bound the mass, force, viscosity and convection terms by $2C_PU_h$, $C_P\sqrt T F$, $2\nu\sqrt T E_h$, and $C_cT^{1/4}U_h^{1/2}E_h^{3/2}$ times $\|v_h\|_V$. This proves the displayed uniform primitive bound.

Let $u_{h,j}^0=P_{Z_j}u_0$. For any $\epsilon>0$, choose $v\in V_\sigma$ with $\|u_0-v\|_2<\epsilon$; the Fortin map satisfies $\Pi_jv\in Z_j$ and $\|\Pi_jv-v\|_2\to0$. Best approximation of the orthogonal projector gives $\|u_{h,j}^0-u_0\|_2\le\|\Pi_jv-u_0\|_2\le\|\Pi_jv-v\|_2+\epsilon$. Letting $j\to\infty$ and then $\epsilon\downarrow0$ proves $u_{h,j}^0\to u_0$ strongly.
Set $G(t)=\int_0^tg(s)\,ds$. By [F5], $G$ is norm-continuous in $V^*$, $G(0)=0$, and $\sup_t\|G(t)\|_{V^*}\le\|g\|_{L^1V^*}$.

The energy theorem [F8] gives $\sum_n\|u_{h,j}^n-u_{h,j}^{n-1}\|_2^2\le C$ uniformly. Therefore $\|\widehat u_{h,j}-\overline u_{h,j}\|_{L^2L^2}^2=\frac13\sum_n\tau_n^j\|u_{h,j}^n-u_{h,j}^{n-1}\|_2^2\le C\tau_{\max,j}\longrightarrow0.$ The pressure bound in step 1.3 is uniform in $j$, so $(P_{h,j})$ is bounded in the separable Hilbert space $L^2(0,T;Q)$. By [A1] and [F7], a further subsequence converges weakly to some $P_*\in L^2(0,T;Q)$. If $K$ is the uniform $L^\infty Q$ bound and $A_\epsilon=\{t:\|P_*(t)\|_2>K+\epsilon\}$ had positive measure, testing weak convergence against $\mathbf1_{A_\epsilon}P_*$ gives $\int_{A_\epsilon}\|P_*(t)\|_2^2\,dt=\lim_j\int_{A_\epsilon}(P_{h,j}(t),P_*(t))_2\,dt\le K\int_{A_\epsilon}\|P_*(t)\|_2\,dt.$ The left side is at least $(K+\epsilon)\int_{A_\epsilon}\|P_*(t)\|_2\,dt$, a contradiction. Hence every $A_\epsilon$ is null and $P_*\in L^\infty Q$ with bound $K$.

Conversely suppose the actual $u_t^{\mathrm{full}}$ is represented in $L^{4/3}(0,T;V^*)$ and set $r=g-u_t^{\mathrm{full}}$. For each $z\in V_\sigma$, the scalar weak equation [F1] gives $r(t)(z)=0$ as a time distribution. The space $V$ is separable: with its equivalent full $H^1$ norm it embeds isometrically into a finite product of scalar $L^2(D)$ spaces by listing each velocity component and its first derivatives; restricting rational-box step functions makes that product separable. The subspace $V_\sigma=\ker\operatorname{div}$ is closed, hence separable (a countable base for the ambient metric space restricts to a countable base on $V_\sigma$, and Countable Choice selects one point from each nonempty base member). For a countable dense family $(z_k)$ in $V_\sigma$, each scalar $r(\cdot)(z_k)\in L^1(0,T)$ is zero almost everywhere by [F6]; outside the countable union of these null sets, continuity of $r(t)\in V^*$ makes it vanish on all of $V_\sigma$.

For every $t$, define the full-test residual $R(t)\in V^*$ by $R(t)(v)=G(t)(v)-(u(t)-u_0,v)_2$. This functional is bounded with $\|R(t)\|_{V^*}\le C_P(U+\|u_0\|_2)+\|g\|_{L^1V^*}$. For each fixed $v\in V$, the scalar map $t\mapsto R(t)(v)$ is continuous: orthogonally project $v$ onto the closed subspace $H_\sigma$; since $u(t)\in H_\sigma$, its pairing with $v$ equals its pairing with that projection and is continuous by [F1].

For the convergence of convection, use the separate Sobolev routes in [F3]: $H^1_0\hookrightarrow L^6$ by the $p=2$ Sobolev exponent in dimension three, and by the $p=3/2$ inequality plus finite-measure Holder in dimension two. Interpolation gives $\|w\|_{L^2L^3}\le\|w\|_{L^2L^2}^{1/2}\|w\|_{L^2L^6}^{1/2}$ and $\|w\|_{L^2L^4}\le\|w\|_{L^2L^2}^{1/4}\|w\|_{L^2L^6}^{3/4}$. The energy bounds give uniform $L^2L^6$ norms, while strong $L^2L^2$ convergence in [F9] therefore implies strong $L^2L^3$ and $L^2L^4$ convergence. For fixed $v\in V$, the gradient term in the skew form pairs weakly convergent gradients with $\overline u_{h,j}\otimes v$ converging strongly in $L^2L^2$; its other term pairs $\nabla v$ with $\overline u_{h,j}\otimes\overline u_{h,j}$ converging strongly in $L^1L^2$, since $\|\overline u_{h,j}\otimes\overline u_{h,j}-u\otimes u\|_{L^1L^2}\le(\|\overline u_{h,j}\|_{L^2L^4}+\|u\|_{L^2L^4})\|\overline u_{h,j}-u\|_{L^2L^4}\to0.$ Replacing $v$ by $\Pi_jv$ changes the integral by at most $C\|\Pi_jv-v\|_V\|\overline u_{h,j}\|_{L^2V}^2$, which tends to zero. No divergence-free property of the test $v$ is used.

Fix $z\in V_\sigma$. The scalar weak equation [F1] says that $(u(t),z)_2$ has distributional derivative $g(t)(z)$ and initial trace $(u_0,z)_2$. Since $g(z)\in L^1$, [F6] gives an absolutely-continuous representative equal to $(u_0,z)_2+G(t)(z)$. Weak continuity in [F1] identifies that representative with $(u(t),z)_2$ for every $t$. Hence $R(t)(z)=0$ for every $z\in V_\sigma$ and every $t$, and $R(0)=0$.

For each $t$, the map $q\mapsto-R(t)(Bq)$ is a bounded real-linear functional on $Q$ of norm at most $C_{\rm div}\|R(t)\|_{V^*}$. Riesz representation [F7] therefore defines a unique $P(t)\in Q$ by $(P(t),q)_2=-R(t)(Bq)$ for all $q\in Q$. The uniform bound from step 3.1 gives the stated $L^\infty Q$ estimate. For fixed $q$, $t\mapsto(P(t),q)_2=-R(t)(Bq)$ is continuous, so $P\in C_w([0,T];Q)$ and $P(0)=0$. Choose a countable orthonormal basis of the separable Hilbert space $Q$. Each finite-coordinate projection of $P$ is strongly measurable because its coordinates are continuous; the projections converge in norm to $P(t)$ at every $t$. For $v\in V$, let $q=\operatorname{div}v\in Q$ by [F2]. Then $v-Bq\in V_\sigma$, so step 4.1 gives $R(t)(v)=R(t)(Bq)=-(P(t),q)_2=b(v,P(t))$. Substitution of the definition of $R$ proves the integrated identity for every $t$ and $v$. If $P_1,P_2$ both satisfy it, set $v=Bq$ for arbitrary $q\in Q$ to obtain $(P_1(t)-P_2(t),q)_2=0$ for every $q$, hence $P_1(t)=P_2(t)$.

The formula $\langle p,\eta\rangle=-\int_0^TP(t)\eta'(t)\,dt$ defines a continuous $Q$-valued distribution because its norm is bounded by $\|P\|_{L^\infty Q}\|\eta'\|_{L^1}$. Differentiating step 6.1 against scalar tests gives $u_t+a_\nu(u,\cdot)+c(u;u,\cdot)+b(\cdot,p)=f$ in $V^*$-valued distributions. If another $Q$-valued distribution has this property, test the difference against $Bq$ for each $q\in Q$; since $\operatorname{div}Bq=q$, the $Q$ inner product of the difference with every $q$ vanishes, so the difference is zero.

Fix $v\in V$ and $\eta\in C_c^\infty(0,T)$. Test the integrated identity of step 1.3 with $\Pi_jv$ and integrate in $t$ against $\eta$. Scalar Fubini rewrites each primitive integral using the bounded weight $s\mapsto\int_s^T\eta(t)\,dt$. Strong convergence of $\widehat u_{h,j}$ from [F9] and step 2.2, strong convergence of initial projections from step 1.4, weak $L^2V$ convergence from [F9], convergence of force averages from [F9], Fortin convergence $\Pi_jv\to v$ in $V$, the convection convergence in step 3.2, and weak convergence $P_{h,j}\rightharpoonup P_*$ pass every term to the limit. In the pressure term, weak convergence of $P_{h,j}$ is paired with the strongly convergent tests $\eta\,\operatorname{div}\Pi_jv\to\eta\,\operatorname{div}v$ in $L^2(0,T;Q)$. The result is the continuous integrated identity of step 6.1 with $P_*$ in place of $P$, as a scalar time distribution.

For fixed $v\in V$, step 6.1 says $(u(t),v)_2+b(v,P(t))=(u_0,v)_2+\int_0^tg(s)(v)\,ds$. The right side is absolutely continuous. Multiply this scalar identity by a $C^1$ time function vanishing near $T$ and integrate by parts; for a finite sum of tests $\varphi(t)=\sum_{k=1}^m\eta_k(t)v_k$ this gives the stated initial-trace formula. Such finite sums are dense in $C^1([0,T];V)$ for tests vanishing near $T$: since $\varphi$ vanishes on a terminal interval, so does $\varphi\prime$. On successively finer partitions, piecewise-linear interpolation of this uniformly continuous derivative has finite-dimensional range, converges uniformly to $\varphi\prime$, and remains zero on a terminal interval. Write an interpolant as $\sum_{k=1}^m\chi_k(t)v_k$ with fixed $v_k\in V$ and continuous piecewise-linear scalar functions $\chi_k$. Then $\varphi_m(t)=-\sum_{k=1}^m\left(\int_t^T\chi_k(s)\,ds\right)v_k$ is a finite sum with $C^1$ scalar coefficients, vanishes near $T$, and converges to $\varphi$ in $C^1$. Every term in the weak-form identity is continuous in that norm by [F1]–[F5], so the identity extends to every stated $\varphi$.

Subtract step 6.1 from the limit identity in step 7.2 and set $v=Bq$ for each $q\in Q$. Then $(P_*-P,q)_2=0$ as a scalar time distribution. Since $P_*-P\in L^2(0,T;Q)$ and $Q$ has a countable dense subset, [F6] and the countable-union result make $P_*=P$ almost everywhere. For $\eta\in C_c^\infty(0,T)$, the identity $\partial_tP_{h,j}=\overline p_{h,j}$ gives $\int_0^T(\overline p_{h,j},q)_2\eta\,dt=-\int_0^T(P_{h,j},q)_2\eta'\,dt\longrightarrow-\int_0^T(P,q)_2\eta'\,dt=(\langle p,\eta\rangle,q)_2.$ This is the claimed weak convergence as $Q$-valued time distributions.

To prove the forward direction of the instantaneous-pressure criterion, suppose $p\in L^{4/3}(0,T;Q)$. The full equation in step 7.1 gives $u_t^{\mathrm{full}}=g-b(\cdot,p)$ as a $V^*$-valued distribution. Since $|\operatorname{div}v|\le\sqrt d\,|\nabla v|$, the map $q\mapsto b(\cdot,q)$ is bounded from $Q$ to $V^*$; [F5] therefore makes $b(\cdot,p)$ Bochner $L^{4/3}V^*$. As $g\in L^{4/3}V^*$ by step 1.2, the actual full derivative has that same regularity.

The continuous residual-recovery lemma [F10] applies to $r\in L^{4/3}(0,T;V^*)$ and gives $p_s\in L^{4/3}(0,T;Q)$ with $r(t)(v)=b(v,p_s(t))$ for all $v\in V$ almost everywhere. Thus $p_s$ is a full pressure distribution for $u$. Uniqueness in step 7.1 identifies $p_s$ with $p$, proving the reverse direction. Therefore the exact necessary-and-sufficient condition is the stated regularity of the actual full derivative.

> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and bounded in one direction: there are a unit vector $e$ and $a<b$ with $a<x\cdot e<b$ for every $x\in\Omega$. Let $1\le p<\infty$. Then $\|u\|_{L^p(\Omega)}\le C(p)\,(b-a)\,\|Du\|_{L^p(\Omega)}$ for every $u\in W^{1,p}_0(\Omega;\mathbb K)$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $p,q\in[1,\infty]$ be
conjugate exponents, and let $f,g$ be measurable real-valued functions.

1. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $q<\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^q(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_p\|g\|_q.$$
2. If $p=1$ and $q=\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$ and
   $g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_1\|g\|_\infty.$$
3. If $p=\infty$ and $q=1$ with $f\in L^\infty(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\|g\|_1.$$

In every case the right-hand side is finite, so $fg$ is integrable.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, $n\ge2$, $1\le p<n$ and $p^{*}=\frac{np}{n-p}$. There is $C(n,p)$ with
$$\|u\|_{L^{p^{*}}(\Omega)}\le C(n,p)\|Du\|_{L^p(\Omega)}$$
for every $u\in W^{1,p}_0(\Omega;\mathbb K)$.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and $X$ a real or complex
Banach space. A strongly measurable function $f:\Omega\to X$ is
**Bochner integrable** if there is a sequence of integrable $X$-valued simple
functions $(s_n)$ such that

$$\lim_{n\to\infty}\int_\Omega\|f-s_n\|\,d\mu=0.$$

For such a sequence define

$$\int_\Omega f\,d\mu:=\lim_{n\to\infty}\int_\Omega s_n\,d\mu.$$

The displayed norm limit exists: the simple integral inequality gives

$$\left\|\int s_n-\int s_m\right\|\leq\int\|s_n-s_m\|\leq\int\|s_n-f\|+\int\|f-s_m\|,$$

so the simple integrals form a Cauchy sequence, and $X$ is complete. The next
theorem proves that the value is independent of the approximating sequence and
characterizes existence by integrability of $\|f\|$.

For $E\in\mathcal A$, write
$\int_Ef\,d\mu:=\int_\Omega\mathbf1_Ef\,d\mu$ whenever this function is
Bochner integrable.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and $X$ a real or complex
Banach space. A function $f:\Omega\to X$ is **strongly measurable** (or
**Bochner measurable**) if there are measurable $X$-valued simple functions
$s_n$ and a measurable null set $N$ such that

$$\lim_{n\to\infty}\|s_n(\omega)-f(\omega)\|=0$$

for every $\omega\in\Omega\setminus N$.

This is a norm-convergence condition. It is not, by definition, merely Borel
measurability of $f$ or measurability of every scalar function $x^*\circ f$.
Changing $f$ on a null set preserves strong measurability: enlarge $N$ by that
null set and retain the same approximants.

Let $f:\Omega\to X$ be strongly measurable. Then $f$ is Bochner integrable if
and only if

$$\int_\Omega\|f\|\,d\mu<\infty.$$

Here an a.e.-defined scalar function is integrated through any measurable
representative supplied by the strong simple approximation. Moreover the
Bochner integral is independent of the approximating sequence in its
definition.

If $f:\Omega\to X$ is Bochner integrable, then for every measurable $E$,

$$\left\|\int_E f\,d\mu\right\|\leq\int_E\|f\|\,d\mu.$$

Let $X,Y$ be Banach spaces, let $T:X\to Y$ be bounded and linear, and let $f$
be Bochner integrable. Then $T\circ f$ is Bochner integrable and, for every
measurable $E$,

$$T\left(\int_Ef\,d\mu\right)=\int_E Tf\,d\mu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $M$ be a closed linear subspace of a real or complex Hilbert space $H$. Then every $x\in H$ has a unique decomposition

$$x=m+n,\qquad m\in M,\quad n\in M^\perp ,$$

so that $H=M\oplus M^\perp$ as a direct sum of the subspace $M$ and its orthogonal complement.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let
$L^2(\mu)$ be the quotient of $\mathcal L^2(\mu)$ by the almost-everywhere zero
functions ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]), with the quotient
norm $\|\cdot\|_2$ ([[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]]).

1. On **real** $L^2(\mu)$ the formula
   $$\langle f,g\rangle:=\int fg\,d\mu$$is a well-defined inner product, linear in both variables, positive definite, with $\langle f,f\rangle=\|f\|_2^2$; with it $L^2(\mu)$ is a real Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]). 2. On **complex** $L^2(\mu;\mathbb C)$ the formula$$\langle f,g\rangle:=\int f\overline g\,d\mu$$
   is a well-defined inner product, linear in the first variable and
   conjugate-linear in the second, positive definite, with
   $\langle f,f\rangle=\|f\|_2^2$; with it $L^2(\mu;\mathbb C)$ is a complex
   Hilbert space ([[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]).

In both cases the inner product induces exactly the established quotient
$L^2$ norm.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice.

Let $1 \le p < \infty$. The finite linear combinations of indicator functions of
half-open boxes with rational endpoints and rational coefficients form a
countable dense subset of $L^p(\mathbb{R}^n)$.

A topological space $X$ is **separable** if some at most countable subset $D\subseteq X$ is dense in $X$ ([[def-dense-top]], [[def-countable]]). Equivalently, every nonempty open subset of $X$ meets $D$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. The map $f\mapsto u_f$, $u_f(\varphi)=\int_\Omega f\varphi$, is a complex-linear injection from $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$ modulo almost-everywhere equality into $\mathcal D'(\Omega)$. It is continuous from the local $L^1$ topology, generated by $f\mapsto\int_K|f|$ for compact $K\subseteq\Omega$, to the strong distribution topology. In particular local $L^1$ convergence implies strong distribution convergence. The continuity estimate itself is choice-free; Countable Choice is used in the cited $L^1$ approximate-identity theorem proving injectivity.

**Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice** ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$(A_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a sequence of subsets of $\mathbb{R}$, each of
measure zero ([[def-measure-zero-and-content-zero]]). Then

$$\bigcup_{n \in \mathbb{N}} A_n \quad \text{has measure zero.}$$

By the padding convention of [[def-measure-zero-and-content-zero]] and
[[def-countable]] the same conclusion covers the union of an at most countable
family of null sets, a finite family being extended by copies of $\varnothing$.

**The hypothesis $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ is spent at exactly one step, step 2.1
below**, where one covering sequence is selected for every $A_n$ at once. Each
$A_n$ has many such covers and nullity provides no rule for singling one out.
Nothing else in the proof selects anything: the diagonal enumeration and the
estimate are formulas.

derivations.claim: To justify pointwise time estimates without strengthening Countable Choice, let $X$ be either $H^2(D)^d$ or $H^1(D)\cap Q$, let $w\in W^{1,\infty}(0,T;X)$, and let $g=w'\in L^\infty(0,T;X)$ be its weak Bochner derivative. The separability of $X$ is [F6]. Define $G(t)=\int_0^tg(s)\,ds$. By [F5], $\|G(t)-G(s)\|_X\le\|g\|_{L^\infty X}|t-s|$. For $\xi\in X$ and $\phi\in C_c^\infty(0,T)$, scalar Fubini gives $-\int_0^T(G(t),\xi)_X\phi'(t)\,dt=-\int_0^T\int_0^t(g(s),\xi)_X\,ds\,\phi'(t)\,dt=\int_0^T(g(s),\xi)_X\phi(s)\,ds.$ Thus $G'=g$ in scalar distributions and $(w-G,\xi)$ has zero distributional derivative.

For $v\in V$, Cauchy–Schwarz for the matrix trace gives $|\operatorname{div}v|=|\operatorname{tr}\nabla v|\le\sqrt d\,|\nabla v|$ almost everywhere. Integrating and applying Cauchy–Schwarz yields $\|b(v,q)\|\le\sqrt d\,\|v\|_V\|q\|_2=M_b\|v\|_V\|q\|_2$, as used in the Statement.

For $q\in H^1(D)\cap Q$, let $I_hq$ be the face-average P1 interpolant from [F3] and set $r_h^0q=I_hq-|D|^{-1}\int_DI_hq$. This belongs to $Q_h$. Since $q$ has mean zero, Cauchy–Schwarz gives $|D|^{1/2}\bigl||D|^{-1}\int_DI_hq\bigr|\le\|I_hq-q\|_2$, hence $\|q-r_h^0q\|_2\le2\|q-I_hq\|_2\le2Ch\|q\|_{H^1(D)}$. Thus some finite uniform best-approximation constant exists, as required by the Statement. Now let $r_h$ be the $L^2$-orthogonal projection onto $Q_h$. The finite-dimensional space $Q_h$ is closed in Hilbert $Q$; [F6] gives its unique orthogonal decomposition. Uniqueness makes $r_h$ linear, and Pythagoras gives $\|r_hq\|_2\le\|q\|_2$, so it is bounded. The Statement's selected best-approximation constant therefore yields $\|q-r_hq\|_2=\inf_{q_h\in Q_h}\|q-q_h\|_2\le C_Ih\|q\|_{H^1(D)}$.

A locally integrable scalar function with zero distributional derivative is constant almost everywhere. Indeed, fix $\rho\in C_c^\infty(0,T)$ with $\int\rho=1$. For any $\phi\in C_c^\infty(0,T)$, $\psi=\phi-(\int\phi)\rho$ has integral zero, so $\theta(t)=\int_0^t\psi(s)\,ds$ belongs to $C_c^\infty(0,T)$ and $\theta'=\psi$. The zero-derivative identity gives $\int(w-G,\xi)\psi=0$, hence $\int(w-G,\xi)\phi=c_\xi\int\phi$ with $c_\xi=\int(w-G,\xi)\rho$. Injectivity of the locally integrable embedding into distributions [F6] yields $(w-G,\xi)=c_\xi$ almost everywhere.

Choose a countable dense set $(\xi_k)$ in $X$. By [F6], the scalar identities in step 2.1 hold outside one common null set. Choose $t_0$ outside that set where the Bochner representative of $w$ is defined, and put $c=w(t_0)-G(t_0)$. Density gives $w(t)-G(t)=c$ for almost every $t$. Thus $w^*(t)=G(t)+c$ is the unique continuous representative and is Lipschitz with constant $\|w'\|_{L^\infty X}$. Apply this to $u$ and $p$: for all $s,t$, $\|u(t)-u(s)\|_V\le M|t-s|$ and $\|p(t)-p(s)\|_{H^1}\le M|t-s|$. Continuity and their essential bounds then give $\|u(t)\|_V\le M_u$ and $\|p(t)\|_{H^1}\le M$ for every $t$. Also $M\ge M_u$, since the $H^2$ norm controls the $V$ norm. These representatives are the ones used for the nodal errors in the existing smooth velocity theorem.

Write $u_n=u(t_n)$, $\overline u_n=\tau_n^{-1}\int_{t_{n-1}}^{t_n}u(t)\,dt$, and use bars similarly for exact pressure, forcing and convection. For each vector in a basis of the finite-dimensional $V_h$, [F1] and step 3.1 imply that the full scalar momentum residual is the zero distribution. All residual terms are integrable, so [F6] identifies that residual with zero almost everywhere; integrating over each time cell and using $u(t_n)-u(t_{n-1})=\int_{t_{n-1}}^{t_n}u_t$ from step 3.1 gives the exact interval equation. Subtract the mixed backward Euler equations and sum through $m$. The identical forcing averages cancel and the time derivatives telescope, giving for every $v_h\in V_h$ $b(v_h,P(t_m)-P_h^m)=-(e_m-e_0,v_h)_2-\sum_{n\le m}\tau_na_\nu(\overline u_n-u_h^n,v_h)-\sum_{n\le m}\tau_n\bigl(\overline{c(u;u,v_h)}_n-c(u_h^n;u_h^n,v_h)\bigr).$ No projection onto the discrete kernel is used in this identity.

Set $R_h^m=\int_0^{t_m}r_hp(t)\,dt\in Q_h$, where $r_h$ is the $L^2$-orthogonal pressure-space projection chosen in step 1.3. Its bounded linearity and [F5] give $\|P(t_m)-R_h^m\|_2\le C_I\int_0^{t_m}h\|p(t)\|_{H^1}\,dt\le C_IThM.$ Apply inf-sup to $R_h^m-P_h^m$, and use $|b(v_h,R_h^m-P(t_m))|\le M_b\|v_h\|_V\|R_h^m-P(t_m)\|_2$. The triangle inequality yields $\|P(t_m)-P_h^m\|_2\le(1+M_b/\beta)C_IThM+\beta^{-1}\sup_{v_h\ne0}\frac{|b(v_h,P(t_m)-P_h^m)|}{\|v_h\|_V}.$

Poincare bounds $|(e_m-e_0,v_h)_2|\le2C_PE_0\|v_h\|_V$. Step 3.1 gives $\|\overline u_n-u_n\|_V\le\tau_nM$, hence $\sum_{n\le m}\tau_n\|\overline u_n-u_h^n\|_V\le\sqrt T E_1+T\tau_{\max}M.$ The viscosity contribution in step 4.1 is therefore at most $2\nu(\sqrt T E_1+T\tau_{\max}M)\|v_h\|_V$.

Trilinearity gives $c(u_n;u_n,v_h)-c(u_h^n;u_h^n,v_h)=c(e_n;u_n,v_h)+c(u_h^n;e_n,v_h).$ Its absolute value is at most $C_c(\|u_n\|_V+\|u_h^n\|_V)\|e_n\|_V\|v_h\|_V$. Weighted Cauchy–Schwarz, $\|u_n\|_V\le M_u$, and [F2] show that its summed contribution is at most $C_c(\sqrt T M_u+M_E)E_1\|v_h\|_V$.

For $t\in(t_{n-1},t_n)$, split $c(u(t);u(t),v_h)-c(u_n;u_n,v_h)=c(u(t)-u_n;u(t),v_h)+c(u_n;u(t)-u_n,v_h).$ By step 3.1, $\|u(t)-u_n\|_V\le\tau_nM$, and $M\ge M_u$. The $V^3$ estimate bounds the integrand by $2C_c\tau_nM^2\|v_h\|_V$. Integrating over the cells through $m$ gives at most $2C_cT\tau_{\max}M^2\|v_h\|_V$, completing the convection bound in step 4.1.

Insert the estimates in steps 5.2, 5.3, and 6.1 into step 5.1. This gives the first displayed pressure-primitive inequality, uniformly in $m$. Substitute $E_0\le C_*H$ and $E_1\le\nu^{-1/2}C_*H$ from [F2]. Since $M\ge1$, both $hM$ and $\tau_{\max}M$ are at most $H$, and $\tau_{\max}M^2\le H$. The resulting coefficient is exactly $K$, so $\max_m\|P(t_m)-P_h^m\|_2\le KH$.

The exact primitive $P$ is Lipschitz in $Q$ with constant at most $\|p\|_{L^\infty Q}\le M$, by step 3.1. Let $\widetilde P$ interpolate its exact endpoint values affinely on the partition. For $t\in[t_{n-1},t_n]$ and $\alpha=(t-t_{n-1})/\tau_n$, $P(t)-\widetilde P(t)=(1-\alpha)(P(t)-P(t_{n-1}))+\alpha(P(t)-P(t_n)),$ so $\|P(t)-\widetilde P(t)\|_2\le2\alpha(1-\alpha)\tau_nM\le\tau_{\max}M$. Convexity gives $\|\widetilde P-P_h\|_{L^\infty Q}\le\max_m\|P(t_m)-P_h^m\|_2$. Together with step 7.1 this proves $\|P-P_h\|_{L^\infty Q}\le(K+1)H$, because $\tau_{\max}M\le H$.

On each time cell, $P_h'=\overline p_h$. Scalar integration by parts against $\eta\in C_c^\infty(0,T)$ and cancellation of the node terms give the $Q$-valued identity $\int_0^T(p-\overline p_h)\eta\,dt=-\int_0^T(P-P_h)\eta'\,dt.$ Scalarization and [F5] justify the vector identity; its norm is at most $\|P-P_h\|_{L^\infty Q}\|\eta'\|_{L^1}$. Step 8.1 proves the stated negative-time-norm estimate.
